Travelling Light on Two Wheels

Not every tour requires a full pannier setup. For weekend getaways, credit card touring, or riders who prefer a minimalist approach, a tail pack or roll bag strapped to the pillion seat provides enough capacity for essentials without the weight and complexity of full luggage systems. The beauty of lightweight touring is the freedom it gives you — the bike handles like normal and you can spontaneously decide to extend your trip.

Tail Packs vs Roll Bags

Tail packs are structured bags that sit on the pillion seat or luggage rack, often with internal compartments and external pockets for organisation. Roll bags are cylindrical waterproof duffels that strap down without any structure — simpler, lighter, and often more waterproof, but harder to organise internally.

What Size Do You Need?

  • 15-20 litres — Enough for a day ride with spare layers, waterproofs, and snacks.
  • 25-35 litres — Perfect for an overnight or weekend trip with a change of clothes and basic toiletries.
  • 40-60 litres — Suitable for a week-long credit card tour if you pack efficiently and use compression bags.

Best Tail Packs and Roll Bags

Kriega US-30 Drypack — The touring community favourite. 30-litre waterproof roll bag with Kriega's hook-loop mounting system. Sits securely without moving and the roll-top closure guarantees waterproofing.

SW-Motech Drybag 350 — A 35-litre waterproof roll bag with welded seams and D-ring straps. Clean cylindrical design that works on virtually any bike.

GIVI UT807C Cargo Bag — A structured 65-litre cargo bag with expandable capacity. Not waterproof on its own but includes a rain cover. Multiple straps keep it secure on the pillion seat.

Oxford Aqua T-50 Roll Bag — Budget 50-litre waterproof roll bag with welded construction. Impressive capacity at a fraction of premium brand prices.

When loading a tail pack, ensure it does not interfere with the rear mudguard, exhaust, or rear light. Secure all straps tightly and check they have not loosened after the first 30 minutes of riding.

Packing Tips

Use packing cubes or dry bags within your tail pack to keep items organised and accessible. Put items you need during the day like waterproofs and snacks at the top. Keep heavy items low and centred. A well-packed tail bag should not shift or bounce even on rough roads.

Security Considerations

Tail packs and roll bags are generally less secure than lockable hard cases. Never leave valuables visible in soft luggage when your bike is unattended. Consider using a small cable lock through the bag handles and around the luggage rack to deter opportunistic theft. For overnight stops, remove your tail pack and take it to your room or tent. The convenience of soft luggage being easy to carry off the bike is also its security weakness at stops. Read our Lightweight Summer Motorcycle Jackets for UK Touring guide for more.
keyTakeaways: Tail packs are structured with pockets for organisation; roll bags are simpler, lighter and often more waterproof.
Size to your trip: 15-20L for a day, 25-35L for a weekend, 40-60L for a week of credit-card touring.
Kriega US-30 Drypack is the community favourite; Oxford Aqua T-50 gives big capacity on a budget.
Use packing cubes or dry bags inside to organise and keep items accessible.
Soft luggage is easy to steal, so remove tail packs at overnight stops and take them with you.

comparisonTable.caption: Tail pack and roll bag sizing

pros: Lightweight minimalist option that keeps the bike handling like normal.
Roll bags with welded seams and roll-top closures are highly waterproof.
Easy to remove and carry off the bike at stops.
cons: Less secure than lockable hard cases.
Roll bags without internal structure are harder to organise.

faq.a: Tail packs are structured bags with internal compartments and external pockets, making them easy to organise, and they sit neatly on the pillion seat or rack. Roll bags are cylindrical waterproof duffels that strap down without internal structure, so they are simpler, lighter and often more waterproof, but harder to organise inside. Choose a tail pack for organisation or a roll bag for outright waterproofing and simplicity.

Match capacity to your trip: 15 to 20 litres carries spare layers, waterproofs and snacks for a day ride; 25 to 35 litres suits an overnight or weekend with a change of clothes and toiletries; and 40 to 60 litres covers a week-long credit-card tour if you pack efficiently with compression bags. Oversizing tempts you to overpack, which raises weight high on the bike.

faq.q: How do I secure a tail pack safely?
faq.a: When loading, make sure the pack does not touch the rear mudguard, exhaust or rear light, then cinch all straps tightly. Check them again after the first thirty minutes of riding, as straps often settle and loosen. A well-packed tail pack should not shift or bounce even on rough roads, so redistribute the load if you feel any movement while riding.

faq.q: Are tail packs secure against theft?
faq.a: No, soft luggage is generally far less secure than lockable hard cases. Never leave valuables visible in a tail pack when the bike is unattended, and consider running a small cable lock through the bag handles and around the luggage rack to deter opportunists. At overnight stops, the simplest security is to remove the tail pack entirely and take it to your room or tent.
